title: Adam (Achitteronose)
summary: Adam, also identified as Achitteronose, was a seventeenth-century western Long Island and Massapequa-associated bilingual envoy.
content:
Adam, also identified as Achitteronose, was a seventeenth-century bilingual envoy associated with western Long Island and Massapequa diplomacy. Records document his work in 1655 and 1656, but the cited sources do not establish his birth or death dates.

The records place him in diplomacy involving Tackapousha and allied western Long Island communities, including Secatogue, Maskinekaug, Merrick, Rockaway, and Canarsie.1

Historical Context

In fall 1655, Adam acted as a bilingual envoy in negotiations for a Rockaway Neck deed with Hempstead officials.1

On March 12, 1656, Adam appears in the mutual protection treaty negotiated with the Dutch at Hempstead by Tackapousha and allied western Long Island leaders.1

Because Adam is documented as an envoy rather than through a full personal biography, the history identifies his documented diplomatic role without assigning him exclusively to a single community.1

References

  1. John A. Strong, The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island from Earliest Times to 1700, pp. 192, 217-218.
  2. Dutch treaty with Tackapousha and western Long Island sachems, March 12, 1656, as discussed by Strong.
why_this_matters: Adam's record shows that Native diplomacy depended on people who could work across languages, communities, and colonial governments. His story preserves western Long Island Native agency in communication, treaty-making, and land negotiation during a period of intense pressure.
activity_update_summary: Newly featured: Adam's documented role as a bilingual envoy in the fall 1655 Rockaway Neck deed negotiations and his participation in the March 1656 mutual-protection treaty at Hempstead.
